title: A Two-Year Calorie Restriction Trial Just Revealed Why You Age Faster Than You Should. The Answer Is in Your Immune System.
excerpt: A landmark Nature Aging study found that cutting 14 per cent of daily calories deactivated complement proteins that drive chronic inflammation — the same proteins that run high in South Asians decades before heart disease strikes.
body:
The search for what slows human ageing just got a concrete answer, and it is not a pill. It is a protein system your body switches on as you get older — one that calorie restriction quietly switches off.

A study published this week in *Nature Aging* analysed blood samples from the CALERIE trial, the first randomised controlled experiment to test long-term calorie restriction in healthy, non-obese humans. Over two years, 220 participants either ate normally or reduced their calorie intake by roughly 14 per cent. The researchers ran unbiased plasma proteomics across both groups and found something they were not specifically looking for.

## The Complement Connection

Calorie restriction significantly lowered multiple complement proteins in the blood, most notably C3a. The complement system, part of the innate immune response, is meant to fight infections. But as we age, it does not quiet down. Instead, it ramps up — driving chronic, low-grade inflammation that researchers call "inflammaging."

The study showed that C3a levels rose steadily with age in both mice and humans. But in the calorie-restricted group, that rise was blunted. The researchers traced the source to visceral adipose tissue — belly fat — where a specific subset of age-associated macrophages produces C3 and feeds an inflammatory loop through the ERK signalling pathway.

When the team inhibited C3a in aged mice, inflammaging markers dropped. Long-lived FGF21 transgenic mice and CR-mimetic PLA2G7 knockout mice also showed lower C3a levels compared to wild-type controls.

## Why South Asians Should Pay Closer Attention

South Asians carry disproportionately higher levels of visceral adipose tissue relative to their body weight, even at a so-called normal BMI. This is not a new finding — the MASALA study at Northwestern has documented it for over a decade. A February 2026 paper from the same cohort showed that South Asian adults in the US develop prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension at significantly higher rates than white and Chinese adults by age 45, despite reporting healthier diets and comparable exercise habits.

The mismatch has puzzled researchers. This complement-inflammaging pathway may be part of the explanation. If visceral fat is the furnace and complement proteins are the smoke, South Asians are starting with a bigger fire — and standard BMI thresholds are not catching it.

## Fasting Traditions That Science Is Catching Up To

Hindu fasting traditions — Ekadashi twice monthly, Navratri nine-day fasts, Karva Chauth, Monday and Thursday vrats — are not calorie restriction trials. But they share a structural feature: periodic, deliberate reductions in food intake that cycle through the year.

Ramadan fasting, which millions of South Asian Muslims observe, similarly compresses eating into a narrow window. A growing body of evidence suggests that even short bouts of calorie reduction can shift complement protein expression, though the CALERIE trial's two-year protocol is the most rigorous demonstration yet.

The study's lead investigators note that the complement system is a "promising, clinically relevant target to reduce inflammaging and prolong healthspan." Translation: this is no longer a longevity hack for biohackers. It is a therapeutic target that drug companies will pursue.

## What This Means for Diaspora Families

For first-generation immigrants who grew up with periodic fasting as a cultural norm and then abandoned it in America, this research may reframe the practice. It is not about religious obligation or willpower theatre. It is about a measurable biological mechanism that your grandmother's calendar may have been modulating all along.

The study does not prove that traditional fasting equals CALERIE-style calorie restriction. But it establishes that even a modest 14 per cent reduction — not starvation, not a crash diet — can deactivate an immune pathway that drives the diseases South Asians fear most: heart disease, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome.

**Sources**: Spadaro, O. et al., *Nature Aging* (2026); Northwestern MASALA study, *Journal of the American Heart Association* (2026); CALERIE Phase-2 trial data, *Nature Aging* (2023).
